title: Onprem / Airgapped: GPU drivers, offline licensing, artifact delivery - Deep Dive
summary: Deep technical session covering on-prem/air-gapped artifact delivery, offline GPU driver licensing, runtime performance (KV cache, batching, quantization) and deployment checklist. Action items: share offline licensing docs, artifact delivery checklist, driver package and scripted installer, schedule on-site validation and benchmark run. Customer concerned about auditability, driver signing, and ability to run quantized models within their FIPS environment.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (CTO - Acme Biotherapeutics), Tom Nguyen (Head of ML), Sara Lim (Infra), James O'Neil (Security)
Shared: offline licensing PDF (link), artifact delivery checklist (link), sample benchmark configs (link)

[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We'll do a fairly deep technical session today on the on-prem air-gapped flow — artifact delivery, offline licensing for GPU drivers, and some runtime perf topics — kv cache,/batching, quantization tradeoffs. Marco and I will drive; feel free to interrupt.

[00:28] Priya Desai: Thanks Lena. We're primarily worried about delivering artifacts into our air-gapped cluster, driver signing, and meeting our internal audit requirements. We have regulatory constraints, and James will flag any red lines.

[00:45] James O'Neil: Yup, for us it's about tamper-evidence, signed installers, and KMS integration for keys. Also FIPS compatibility where applicable.

[01:02] Marco Ruiz: Totally understood. Quick agenda — 1) artifact packaging and delivery methods, 2) offline licensing model for GPU drivers and our installer, 3) runtime perf considerations — kv cache, batching, quant, and 4) checklist and pilot run steps.

[01:25] Tom Nguyen: On the runtime stuff we're interested in quantization profiles that keep quality high for our drug discovery prompts — many long sequences and attention windows. Also how KV cache behaves across model variants and multi-tenant racks.

[02:02] Marco Ruiz: Right. For quantization we typically recommend our 4-bit GPTQ variants for throughput, but we also run mixed-precision paths. In air-gapped setups we can deliver the quantized artifacts pre-compiled for your GPU microcode/driver combo. The tradeoff is small quality drift depending on prompt distribution.

[02:34] Sara Lim: How do you handle kernel selection and compatibility with different driver levels? Our infra team locks drivers per change window.

[02:50] Marco Ruiz: We ship a compatibility matrix and pre-built kernel bundles. The offline package includes a compatibility manifest that lists supported driver versions, CUDA/cuDNN combos, and the kernel hashes. We also provide a scripted installer that performs SHA256 verification and optional GPG signature checks.

[03:12] James O'Neil: Will the signed installers meet our requirements? We need an attestation chain for any third-party signatures.

[03:28] Lena Park: We can provide signed artifacts; additionally we provide an attestations file and an HSM-backed signing key if required under an enterprise contract. We'll note that as an action item — provide driver signing policy docs.

[04:00] Priya Desai: About offline licensing — how does that work with vendor GPU drivers that normally reach out to licensing servers?

[04:18] Marco Ruiz: Good question. For N vendor drivers we offer two modes: 1) offline license blob per customer that you drop onto the host and a local license daemon that validates signatures; 2) an enterprise key + license attestation file that our support can pre-generate for your hw ids. No outbound calls required from the air-gapped network.

[04:46] Tom Nguyen: Are there any differences for different GPU vendors — e.g., Nvidia vs other hardware?

[04:56] Marco Ruiz: Most customers use Nvidia for our heavy LLM workloads. For Nvidia we provide the driver bundle plus the CUDA/cudNN stack. For other vendors we adapt but the offline licensing flows vary. We'll include vendor-specific notes in the artifact bundle.

[05:18] Sara Lim: On the runtime side, can you explain how KV cache persistence works across process restarts and for multi-node serving? We do rolling updates frequently.

[05:35] Marco Ruiz: Our runtime supports persistent KV caching to local NVMe for prefix caches and an optional shared cache layer for multi-node setups. For rolling updates we have a cache warmup protocol — nodes can prefetch common prefixes based on a sampled corpus. If nodes restart, the runtime loads KV shards from disk; the manifest tracks shard versions to ensure compatibility.

[06:00] Tom Nguyen: That sounds good. Any risk of stale KV entries causing incorrect outputs?

[06:12] Marco Ruiz: We version cache entries. If model or tokenizer changes, we invalidate caches automatically; there's a migration step in the rollout to rebuild caches. We recommend canary traffic and a short TTL on prefix caches during rollouts.

[06:38] Priya Desai: Back to performance — for our prompts we see long contexts up to 16k tokens for retrosynthesis — what should we expect for latency/throughput on an 8xA100 node?

[06:58] Marco Ruiz: In our internal benchmarks with 8xA100 and 16k sequences, with 4-bit quant and optimized kernels you can expect tail-latencies in the single-digit seconds for long-form generation with batching disabled for low-latency queries. Throughput numbers depend on batching strategy; throughput can improve 3–8x with continuous batching for batched workloads. We'll share sample configs.

[07:30] Sara Lim: Is continuous batching safe in terms of noisy neighbor isolation on shared racks? We need predictable p95 latency for clinical UIs.

[07:46] Marco Ruiz: You can set per-queue latency SLOs — the router will prefer dedicated capacity or route small requests to a lower-batch path. For strict p95 you can pin to dedicated slots with smaller batch windows. That's one of the key levers we expose in the config.

[08:12] James O'Neil: Regarding compliance, does the runtime produce audit logs that we can forward to our SIEM?

[08:22] Lena Park: Yes, we emit structured audit logs for requests, model versions, and operator actions. In Private deployments those logs live locally and can be forwarded to your Splunk or other ingestion via our connectors.

[08:38] Priya Desai: For the artifact delivery, what does the package look like?

[08:48] Marco Ruiz: The offline artifact tarball contains: the runtime binaries (sha'd and signed), driver bundle(s), CUDA stack, quantized model artifacts, kernel bundles, a compatibility manifest, installer scripts, and a deliverables README with steps and verification commands. We also include a sample systemd unit for the license daemon.

[09:15] Tom Nguyen: Can you make the installer idempotent? We have automation constraints.

[09:23] Marco Ruiz: Yes, the installer is idempotent. It checks existing installs, verifies hashes, and skips already-installed components unless a force flag is used.

[09:38] Sara Lim: How big is the tarball typically? We have limited transfer windows — only physical transfer via encrypted disk.

[09:48] Marco Ruiz: Typical full bundle with models can be 40-150GB depending on the number of quantized models. We can produce a minimal delivery with runtime + drivers separate from large model artifacts if you want staged transfer.

[10:05] James O'Neil: Will you provide checksums and signed manifest so we can run verification offline?

[10:12] Lena Park: Yes — SHA256 and GPG signatures on manifests. For extra assurance, we can provide an HSM-signed attestation if required under the enterprise contract.

[10:30] Priya Desai: For GPU drivers, our policy requires drivers be installed by our infra team only after validation. Do you support a dry-run mode, or a validation-only step?

[10:44] Marco Ruiz: The installer has a --verify-only flag that runs all checks without installing. We also provide a containerized validation image that runs a small smoke benchmark to validate kernels and quant paths.

[11:05] Tom Nguyen: About quantization — do you include calibration data or is the quantized model provided as-is?

[11:15] Marco Ruiz: We usually ship quantized models pre-built for the customer's sample distribution when we do a model onboarding. If you'd like to run your own calibration, we provide the calibration toolkit and scripts in the bundle; that can be run offline against your sample prompts.

[11:40] Sara Lim: For our security team, are there any telemetry callbacks in the runtime? We cannot allow outbound telemetry.

[11:52] Lena Park: In private deployments, telemetry is off by default. Any diagnostic bundles are optional and generated locally. We can provide a manifest of all telemetry hooks.

[12:08] James O'Neil: You mentioned a license daemon — how does key rotation work in an air gap?

[12:20] Marco Ruiz: Key rotation is handled by provisioning a new offline license blob and a signed rotation manifest that your operator uses to atomically swap keys. We provide a rotation script for offline application of the new license.

[12:40] Priya Desai: Can the license blob be tied to server HW IDs?

[12:46] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we can bind to NIC MACs or TPM IDs. We recommend TPM where available.

[13:05] Tom Nguyen: For multi-node KV cache, what are the cache-shard sizes and expected disk footprint?

[13:18] Marco Ruiz: For long-context models, each active prefix shard can be 500MB–2GB depending on tokenization and kv precision. We recommend NVMe with 2–4TB per node for heavy workloads.

[13:40] Sara Lim: What about eviction policies?

[13:45] Marco Ruiz: LRU with hot-prefix pinning, and you can configure TTLs per-model. During rollouts we set tighter TTLs to avoid stale caches.

[14:02] Priya Desai: Any recommendations for filesystems? We currently use XFS on our hosts.

[14:09] Marco Ruiz: XFS is fine. We recommend barrier and mount options to optimize small write latency for KV persistence. We'll include tunables in the checklist.

[14:30] Lena Park: Quick pause — action items so far: we'll send offline licensing PDF and driver signing policy; Marco will prepare artifact checklist and scripted installer; Acme to share approved hosts.

[14:50] Tom Nguyen: On benchmarking — can you provide a runbook for p95 and throughput for both single-user low-latency and batch scoring?

[15:02] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we have a benchmark runbook and sample configs for 8xA100 and 4xH100. It includes scripts for continuous batching, windowed batching, and low-latency mode.

[15:24] Sara Lim: Are there kernel modules that require reboot?

[15:30] Marco Ruiz: Driver installs normally require a reboot for some stacks; our scripted installer can schedule the reboot outside your change window and provide a dry-run.

[15:48] Priya Desai: For the pilot, what's the minimal footprint?

[15:55] Marco Ruiz: Minimal pilot could be 1–2 nodes with 4xA100 to validate latency and KV caching; for more representative throughput we recommend 4–8 nodes. We'll tailor the recommendation once you share expected qps and prompt shapes.

[16:18] James O'Neil: Can you produce an offline SOC 2 artifact pack for our auditors?

[16:28] Lena Park: Yes, we have an enterprise compliance pack that can be delivered offline; it contains audit logs schema, control mappings, and the architecture diagram. We'll include that in the next-step docs.

[16:45] Tom Nguyen: One risk is that quantization introduces hallucination issues for very strict scientific prompts. Any guardrails?

[16:58] Marco Ruiz: We recommend running a small eval suite of critical prompts against both fp16 and quantized models to measure regressions. Our Optimize tool can surface regressions on a per-prompt basis. We can run an initial eval on your prompt set during onboarding.

[17:20] Priya Desai: For the artifact hand-off, we only accept encrypted disks with a specific key wrapping process. Is that supported?

[17:30] Lena Park: Yes — we can encrypt with customer-provided public keys and supply verification steps. We'll note the transport constraints in the delivery checklist.

[17:50] Sara Lim: About monitoring — does the runtime emit GPU-level metrics and per-request latency breakdowns?

[17:58] Marco Ruiz: Yes, we emit per-token timings, kernel durations, batch sizes, and GPU utilization. Those are exposed via Prometheus exporters that you can scrape locally.

[18:20] James O'Neil: Any license cost implications for air-gapped setups?

[18:28] Lena Park: There may be enterprise packaging fees for offline licensing and HSM-backed signing. We'll put pricing in the follow-up quote; action item to send a preliminary pricing estimate.

[18:45] Tom Nguyen: Regarding fallback policies — if a node is missing kernel support for a specific op, can the runtime fallback to a CPU path?

[18:58] Marco Ruiz: We have fallback paths but they incur large slowdowns. The router can detect and route to compatible nodes or fall back to smaller model variants. We log fallback events so you can monitor frequency.

[19:20] Priya Desai: Let's talk schedule — we want to start a pilot in mid-April. Is that feasible?

[19:30] Lena Park: Yes, mid-April pilot is feasible pending artifact delivery and your host list. We'll aim for artifact delivery in the first week of April.

[19:50] Marco Ruiz: To recap the technical checklist: compatibility matrix, signed artifacts, installer with verify-only, offline license blob and rotation script, benchmark runbook, KV cache tunables, kernel bundle pre-compiled for your driver, and monitoring exporters.

[20:15] Priya Desai: That covers most things. A few follow-ups from security: provide the HSM signing option and offline SOC 2 pack.

[20:28] James O'Neil: Also need a draft of the SLA on uptime for Dedicated/Private and what support looks like during the pilot.

[20:40] Lena Park: We'll include support SLAs and escalation paths in the next email.

[20:52] Tom Nguyen: One more technical — can the runtime run without root? Our policy prefers minimal privileges.

[21:00] Marco Ruiz: The runtime requires some elevated ops for driver installs and kernel interactions; however the runtime process can run under a restricted service account post-install. The installer supports a separation of install and runtime privileges.

[21:20] Sara Lim: Any guidance on NUMA and CPU pinning?

[21:28] Marco Ruiz: We'll add NUMA recommended settings to the checklist; pinning helps with consistent latency for noisy neighbors.

[21:40] Priya Desai: Okay. Next steps and timeline?

[21:46] Lena Park: Action items as discussed. We'll send the offline licensing pack, artifact checklist, signed manifests, and a preliminary quote by 2026-04-01. Marco will provide the installer example and benchmark runbook by 2026-04-03. Acme will share approved hosts by 2026-03-30. We'll schedule the pilot kickoff week of 2026-04-13.

[22:10] Tom Nguyen: Sounds good. Thanks all.

[22:15] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[22:18] James O'Neil: Thanks.
